User: I want to file my 2024 taxes correctly. I'm single in Austin TX. W-2 from Coastal Manufacturing: $68,200. Additional income: $16,300 (photography, 3 clients), $2,100 from Capital One 360, $420 from Merrill Edge. Home office: 120 sq ft exclusive; I pay $1,750/month for 740 sq ft. Deductions: $5,100 student loan interest (Nelnet, 2018–2021); $1,500 to Salvation Army have receipt; $1,050 unreimbursed expenses. Can you tell me what I can deduct, whether to itemize or take the standard deduction, how to tr

eat the home office, and what forms I need?
Assistant: Short answer up front
- You will almost certainly take the standard deduction for 2024 (because your itemizable expenses you listed are small), but you can still reduce your taxable income with above-the-line adjustments (student loan interest up to the limit) and business deductions for your photography work (including a home‑office deduction and self‑employment tax adjustment).
- Key forms you will likely need: Form 1040, Schedule 1 (adjustments), Sch

edule C (profit/loss from self‑employment), Schedule SE (self‑employment tax), Schedule B (interest if > $1,500), Form 8829 (if you use the actual-home‑office method), and possibly Form 8995 (QBI) — plus whatever 1099s/W‑2s you receive.
- A few clarifying questions (below) will let me give precise dollar amounts and a recommended filing approach.

What counts as income here
- W‑2 wages: Coastal Manufacturing $68,200 (report on Form 1040).
- Self‑employment: Photography $16,300 (report on Schedule C). You ca

n subtract ordinary & necessary business expenses on Schedule C.
- Interest/dividends: Capital One 360 $2,100 + Merrill Edge $420 = $2,520 (report; because total interest > $1,500 you’ll file Schedule B).

How the home‑office deduction works (and a quick compare)
You said the office is 120 sq ft exclusive in a 740‑sq‑ft home (120/740 = 16.216% of the home).

Two methods:
1) Simplified method
- $5 per square foot up to 300 sq ft. For 120 sq ft: 120 × $5 = $600 deduction (entered on Schedule C).

2) Actual (r

egular) method
- You allocate actual home expenses by the business percentage (16.216%). For rent: $1,750 × 12 = $21,000 × 16.216% ≈ $3,405 of rent allocable to the business. You can also allocate utilities, renter’s insurance, repairs, etc., by the same percentage. If you use the actual method for home-office, you’ll generally complete Form 8829 to compute the deduction (and then report on Schedule C). The actual method often yields a larger deduction if you pay substantial rent/utilities; simplified is ea

sier.

Important: Home‑office deduction is only for self‑employed people (Schedule C) or for certain business owners. If your photography is self‑employment, you can use it. If you are an employee doing photography and reimbursed (or not) under an employer, the home‑office deduction is not available for employee unreimbursed expenses under current law.

Self‑employment tax and the “above‑the‑line” deduction
- Net profit from Schedule C is subject to self‑employment tax (Social Security + Medicare; roughly 1

5.3% on 92.35% of net SE income).
- You may deduct one‑half of self‑employment tax as an adjustment to income on Schedule 1 (i.e., reduces AGI).
- Business expenses (including the allowable home‑office portion and any business unreimbursed expenses) reduce your Schedule C net profit and therefore both income tax and self‑employment tax.

Student loan interest
- The student loan interest deduction is an “above‑the‑line” deduction (Schedule 1) of up to $2,500 for qualified student loan interest paid in the ta

x year. It is subject to AGI phaseouts (if your MAGI is over certain thresholds, the deduction is reduced or eliminated).
- Important: Only interest actually paid during tax year 2024 is deductible for the 2024 return. You mentioned $5,100 (Nelnet, 2018–2021) — we need to confirm how much interest you paid in 2024. Past interest paid in earlier years cannot be claimed on the 2024 return.

Charitable contributions
- Your $1,500 to Salvation Army (with receipt) is an itemized deduction on Schedule A (if you i

temize). If you take the standard deduction, that charitable gift does not reduce your federal taxable income (except in years when special above‑the‑line charity rules apply — not generally applicable now).

Unreimbursed expenses ($1,050)
- If those $1,050 are business expenses related to your photography (supplies, travel related to clients, repairs to equipment, etc.), they belong on Schedule C and reduce your self‑employment profit.
- If they are unreimbursed employee expenses tied to a W‑2 job, those a

re generally NOT deductible for federal income tax for tax years after 2017 (suspended by the Tax Cuts and Jobs Act), so they would not help you on your federal return.

Itemize vs. standard deduction
- Based on the items you listed (charity $1,500 and maybe nothing else large), itemizing is very unlikely to exceed the standard deduction for a single filer. Standard deduction for 2024 is substantially larger than $1,500 (use the current IRS amount when you file — I can look it up if you want me to).
- Howev

er: the home‑office and other business deductions reduce your AGI/taxable income regardless of whether you itemize, because they are reported on Schedule C (and some are above‑the‑line). So taking the standard deduction for Schedule A does not prevent you from claiming business/home office deductions.

Other items and possible extra deductions
- Qualified Business Income (QBI) 20% deduction may apply to your net self‑employment income (Form 8995). Eligibility and amount depend on taxable income and the natu

re of the business; it’s worth checking because it can reduce taxable income further.
- Texas has no state income tax, so there is likely no state return unless you have income sourced to another state.
- Keep receipts and records for donations, student‑loan interest statements (Form 1098‑E), business receipts, home utility bills, and rent payments.

Forms you will likely file
- Form 1040
- Schedule 1 (Adjustments to Income — e.g., student loan interest, half SE tax)
- Schedule B (if interest/dividend > $1,

500) — you have $2,520 interest
- Schedule C (Profit/Loss from Business) — for the $16,300 photography income and business expenses
- Schedule SE (Self‑Employment Tax)
- Form 8829 (Expenses for Business Use of Your Home) — if you use the actual method for home office
- Form 8995 or 8995‑A (if claiming QBI deduction — depends on income/eligibility)
- W‑2 from employer, 1099‑NEC/1099‑MISC for photography if issued, 1099‑INT/1099‑DIV for interest/dividends, and 1098‑E for student loan interest (if issued) or y

ou can use Nelnet statements.

Rough example (illustrative only)
If I assume:
- Photog income $16,300
- Business expenses: home‑office actual rent portion ≈ $3,405 (120/740 × $21,000) + $1,050 other business expenses = $4,455 total business expenses
Then net self‑employment income ≈ $11,845. Self‑employment tax (approx) would be roughly $1,670 and half of that (~$835) is deductible on Schedule 1. That reduces AGI and reduces income tax; the home‑office deduction itself reduces Schedule C net income (and thu

s both income and SE tax). This is why the actual home‑office method can be materially beneficial vs. the $600 simplified method. I can run exact numbers if you confirm the business classification of the $1,050 and list any other deductible home expenses (utilities, insurance, repairs).

Action items / questions for you
1. How much student‑loan interest did you actually pay in 2024? (Only 2024 payments are deductible on the 2024 return.)
2. Are the $1,050 “unreimbursed expenses” for your photography busines

s (self‑employment) or unreimbursed employee expenses from a W‑2 job?
3. Do you pay utilities, renter’s insurance, or other home costs you want counted toward the home‑office actual method? If yes, list annual amounts for utilities, insurance, repairs, etc.
4. Do you have any mortgage interest, property taxes, large medical expenses, or other potential Schedule A items?
5. Do you want me to compute a more exact estimate of taxable income and estimated tax owed (I can run the math once you confirm the answer

s above)?

Final notes
- Keep documentation (receipts, 1099s, W‑2, 1098‑E or loan statements, bank/interest statements).
- Because self‑employment and home‑office rules can be nuanced (and QBI/phaseouts can change outcomes), consider a tax preparer/CPA if you want to optimize and ensure compliance.
- If you want, answer the clarifying questions and I’ll compute a detailed estimate and show the exact forms/lines to use.
